title: Four Players With Indian Roots Are at This World Cup. It Has Never Happened Before.
excerpt: From a Punjabi midfielder who trained at Bayern Munich to a 19-year-old Keralite winger in Qatar's squad, the diaspora is represented at football's biggest stage for the first time at this scale.
body:
India has never played at a senior men's FIFA World Cup. The Blue Tigers crashed out in the second round of qualifying for the 2026 edition, extending a drought that stretches back to 1950, when they withdrew after qualifying. But when the tournament kicked off in Mexico City on Wednesday, the country's diaspora was already represented on the pitch — and by the time the group stage ends, four players with Indian roots will have taken the field across three continents.

It is the first time this many Indian-origin footballers have appeared at a single World Cup. Their stories span Punjab, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Guadeloupe, and they play for nations as far apart as New Zealand and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

## Sarpreet Singh — New Zealand

The most prominent of the four is Sarpreet Singh, a 27-year-old attacking midfielder who wears the number 10 shirt for the All Whites. Born in Auckland to Punjabi parents from Jalandhar, Singh was enrolled at the Wynton Rufer Soccer Academy at seven by his mother Sarabjit, who drove him to training sessions when most Indian parents in New Zealand were steering their children toward more conventional careers.

Singh rose through local clubs Papatoetoe and Onehunga Sports before joining Wellington Phoenix's academy at 15. His performances at the 2019 FIFA U-20 World Cup earned him a three-year contract with Bayern Munich, making him the first player of Indian heritage to represent the German giants. Injury-plagued spells at Nürnberg, Hansa Rostock and clubs in Portugal and Serbia followed before he returned to Wellington Phoenix in early 2026.

"I don't say it's added pressure," Singh told *Livemint* from Miami ahead of the tournament. "I just want to do my best to lift the names of Indian people, and there is no better stage to do it than the World Cup."

New Zealand play Iran in their opener on June 15 at the Los Angeles Stadium in Inglewood, followed by Egypt and Belgium. They are the lowest-ranked side in Group G at 85th, but Singh is undaunted. "We don't have anything to be afraid of," he said.

## Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid — Qatar

At 19, Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid is the youngest of the four. Born in Doha to Malayali parents from Kannur, Kerala, his father Jamshid played football for the University of Calicut before moving to Qatar in 1996 and now works as an accountant.

Tahsin trained at Qatar's Aspire Academy before joining Al Duhail, where he emerged as one of the country's most explosive young attackers. A winger with blistering pace, he has represented Qatar at senior, U-23, U-20 and youth levels. His senior debut came during a World Cup qualifier against Afghanistan in June 2024.

He is the first player holding an Indian passport connection to feature at a World Cup for Qatar, a detail that has not gone unnoticed among Kerala's football-mad fanbase.

## Nishan Velupillay — Australia

Nishan Velupillay, 25, was born and raised in Melbourne. His father Sasinath is of Sri Lankan Tamil descent with Malaysian roots, and his mother Gillian is Anglo-Indian. He attended Mazenod College in Mulgrave and started at Glen Eira FC before working his way through Melbourne Victory's academy.

The forward scored on his international debut, coming off the bench against China and netting within minutes to seal a 3-1 win in a World Cup qualifier. He has earned seven senior caps and scored three goals. Australia open their campaign against Turkey in Vancouver on June 14, then face the United States in Seattle on June 19 — a match that will draw enormous Indian-American interest.

## Samuel Moutoussamy — DR Congo

The least obvious Indian connection belongs to Samuel Moutoussamy, a central midfielder for DR Congo. Born in France, his father comes from a South Indian Tamil family in Guadeloupe — a lineage that traces back through the French Caribbean to Tamil Nadu. His consistent displays in European club football and tireless work rate in African qualifiers made him an indispensable starter for Congo.

## What It Means for Indian Football

None of these four players wear India's jersey. But their presence at the world's biggest sporting event carries an emotional weight that transcends national team borders. For the 1.4 billion people who have never seen their country at a World Cup, watching players with roots in Jalandhar, Kannur and Chennai compete against the world's best changes the relationship with the tournament from spectator to stakeholder.

"I see it as a responsibility to do my best and even inspire the next generation," Singh said. An Indian flag will be quietly flying at football's grandest stage this summer — four times over.
